questions.scenario: A team starts designing a new customer portal from a blank page, and the first review is expected to take three weeks.
questions.stem: What would shorten the review and improve the design?
options: Starting from the closest Azure Architecture Center reference architecture and reviewing only the deviations, each recorded in an ADR
Adding more reviewers
Skipping the review for internal portals
Copying the last project's design exactly
questions.explanation: A maintained baseline answers most questions already; the review focuses on where and why this design differs. Copying an old project carries its unexamined assumptions.

questions.scenario: One team of six will build the wholesale portal. A proposal splits it into nine microservices on AKS.
options: Nine microservices, to be ready for scale
A modular monolith with strict module boundaries on App Service or Container Apps, extracting a service only when another team needs to own it
One large project with no internal structure
Serverless functions for every endpoint
questions.explanation: Microservices pay off when several teams must ship independently. For one team, a modular monolith keeps operations simple and keeps the option to split later.

questions.scenario: Workload teams create their own subscriptions, networks and logging, and the security team finds a different configuration every time.
options: A monthly security audit
One subscription for everything
An Azure landing zone: a platform team owns the hub, identity, logging and policy, and workloads get vended subscriptions as spokes that inherit it
A wiki page of recommended settings
questions.explanation: Shared concerns built once and inherited through management groups and vending make every new subscription consistent. Audits and wikis find drift after it happens instead of preventing it.

questions.scenario: The platform team wants to require private endpoints on all SQL databases across 30 existing subscriptions.
questions.stem: How should it roll this out?
options: Deny immediately so nothing new slips through
Ask teams to comply by the end of the quarter
Apply it to new subscriptions only
Assign the policy in Audit at the management group, fix the findings with owners and dates, then switch to Deny, with time-limited exemptions for real exceptions
questions.explanation: Audit reveals the impact without breaking live deployments; Deny then keeps the estate compliant. Denying first blocks teams and pushes them to work around the platform.

questions.scenario: The monthly Azure bill has grown 60% and nobody can say which products caused it.
questions.stem: What is the foundation for answering?
options: Required tags such as app, owner and cost-centre enforced by policy, budgets per subscription with anomaly alerts, and a monthly showback per team from Cost Management
Cutting every team's budget by 60%
Buying reservations for everything
Moving to a cheaper region
questions.explanation: FinOps starts with allocation: consistent tags and per-subscription budgets show who spends what, so the right team can act. Blanket cuts and blind commitments do not explain the growth.

questions.scenario: A data-centre exit is due in twelve months. The estate includes 60 VMs, 10 SQL Server instances and 12 IIS web apps.
questions.stem: Which plan is most likely to meet the date and cut running cost?
options: Rewrite every app as microservices, then migrate
Rehost everything exactly as specified on site and review costs in a few years
Assess with Azure Migrate, retire what is unused, rehost most VMs right-sized, replatform web apps to App Service and SQL to Managed Instance, and modernise selectively after the move
Migrate only the databases and keep the apps on site
questions.explanation: A strategy per workload meets the deadline while capturing cheap wins. Rewrites miss dates, and unchanged rehosting from on-site specifications usually costs more than the data centre did.

questions.scenario: The first migration wave moved an app, which then failed because it relied on a file share that was still on site.
questions.stem: What should the next waves do differently?
options: Move everything in one weekend
Group workloads by dependency analysis so things that talk to each other move together, and test-migrate each wave in an isolated network before cutover
Keep file shares on site permanently
Skip test migrations to save time
questions.explanation: Dependency data shows what must move together, and test migrations catch missing pieces before users do. A big-bang weekend multiplies the blast radius.

questions.scenario: A migrated monolith needs its pricing engine rebuilt, but the business cannot accept a risky cut-over.
options: The strangler fig pattern: route pricing through a façade, build the new service alongside, switch the route, and roll back by switching it back
A full rewrite of the monolith first
Freeze the monolith for a year
Run both systems and let users choose
questions.explanation: Replacing one capability at a time behind a façade delivers value early and keeps every step reversible.

questions.scenario: Store tills and the warehouse system must stay on site, but compliance wants them patched and monitored like Azure resources.
options: A separate management tool per site
Moving them to Azure anyway
Azure Arc, bringing them under Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor and update management
A VPN to each site
questions.explanation: Arc extends Azure's management plane to machines outside Azure. A VPN connects networks but governs nothing.

questions.scenario: A lead wants to certify a team of developers, platform engineers and two future architects in the coming year.
options: Everyone takes AZ-900 and stops there
Everyone takes AZ-305 directly
Certifications by role - AZ-204 for developers, AZ-104 then AZ-700 or AZ-500 for platform engineers, AZ-104 then AZ-305 for the architects - studied by building in sandbox subscriptions
Whichever exam has the best pass rate on dump sites
questions.explanation: Role-matched certifications reflect the work people do; AZ-305 requires AZ-104. Building in sandboxes produces real skill, and dumps can get certifications revoked.

questions.scenario: Twice this year the team learnt about a service retirement from a production failure.
questions.stem: Which practice prevents a third time?
options: Recertifying everyone
Watching Service Health, Advisor and Azure Updates retirement notices, and a monthly 'what changed that affects us' session with owned actions
Avoiding new services
Reading documentation once a year
questions.explanation: Retirements are announced well in advance; a regular, owned habit turns notices into planned work.

questions.scenario: A design for the partner API says it will be 'enterprise-grade and scalable'.
questions.stem: What should the review require first?
options: A premium tier for every component
A list of the partners
Numbers: availability target, RTO and RPO, p95 latency at a stated peak, per-partner rate limits, data residency and a monthly cost ceiling
An AKS cluster
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements as numbers make a design testable. Without them, reviews become arguments about adjectives.

questions.scenario: To launch on time, the team will skip zone redundancy for its database. The review agrees.
options: Record the decision and trade-off in an ADR and the technical debt register, with the accepted risk and the trigger for adding zone redundancy
Nothing; the review agreed
Tell only the database administrator
Add zone redundancy anyway after launch without telling anyone
questions.explanation: An agreed shortcut is still a risk the business carries. Recording it, with what forces repayment, keeps it a decision rather than a forgotten gap.

questions.scenario: Design reviews at Northline run long, are dominated by one senior engineer, and leave no record.
options: Let the senior engineer approve designs alone
Replace reviews with a checklist email
Hold reviews only for failed projects
A short design document read beforehand; 60 minutes walking the Well-Architected pillars plus a pre-mortem; ADRs, owned actions and a verdict recorded; chairing rotated across leads
questions.explanation: Structure - pillars, a timebox and a pre-mortem - moves the conversation from volume to evidence; records and owned actions make it stick; rotating the chair spreads the skill.
